message_text:
I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030.

This is Real Hope, Real Change — a practical, fair step that cuts bills, cleans our air, and protects young people’s future. Petrol cars lock us into volatile fuel prices and massive health costs from air pollution; switching to zero-emission vehicles and better public transport would save families money and reduce climate-wrecking emissions. But the transition must be fair. The government should combine the ban with a massive programme of support: free or heavily subsidised public charging, grants and low-cost loans for electric cars, and an urgent national home insulation and retrofit drive so people don’t pay to heat wastefully powered homes. We should also expand affordable, safe alternatives — free bus and tram travel for under-25s, investment in local rail, and safer streets for walking and cycling. Tackle the real villains—fossil fuel interests and profiteering car corporations—so the benefits go to communities, not shareholders. For the common good: ban new petrol cars by 2030, backed by a just transition that leaves no one behind.

We oppose any government diktat to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This is another top-down Brussels-style edict dressed up as “green” virtue-signalling that will punish ordinary people far more than it helps the planet. Working families, rural communities and small businesses rely on reliable, affordable petrol vehicles — not electric cars that cost a fortune, have patchy range, and leave drivers stranded in places without chargers. Forcing a 2030 ban will wreck the used car market, smash family budgets, and deepen the cost-of-living crisis while lining the pockets of global corporations and handing control to remote regulators. Instead of imposing blanket bans, government should scrap green levies, invest in practical British energy and charging infrastructure, and let consumers choose. Real help is cutting fuel costs, boosting North Sea energy, and protecting farming and rural livelihoods — not launching a social experiment that risks turning Net Zero into Net Poverty. Scrap the 2030 ban and put common sense back in charge.

Working families, rural communities and small businesses rely on reliable, affordable petrol vehicles — not electric cars that cost a fortune, have patchy range, and leave drivers stranded in places without chargers. Forcing a 2030 ban will wreck the used car market, smash family budgets, and deepen the cost-of-living crisis while lining the pockets of global corporations and handing control to remote regulators. Instead of imposing blanket bans, government should scrap green levies, invest in practical British energy and charging infrastructure, and let consumers choose. Real help is cutting fuel costs, boosting North Sea energy, and protecting farming and rural livelihoods — not launching a social experiment that risks turning Net Zero into Net Poverty. Scrap the 2030 ban and put common sense back in charge.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. This is a bold, practical step that tackles the climate emergency while cutting household costs and improving health. Electric vehicles and active travel are ready now — renewables are the cheapest power we have, and accelerating the switch will reduce fuel bills and end our dependence on volatile fossil markets that make life harder for renters, workers and families.

But a ban must be fair. We should pair it with massive investment in affordable, reliable public transport, rapid home charging and retrofit grants so no one is left behind. Prioritise grants for low‑income households, public fleets, and community-led transport schemes rather than subsidies for oil companies or luxury tax breaks. Combine the ban with free bus travel for young people and better walking and cycling routes to make cleaner choices the easiest choices.

This is about Real Hope, Real Change — a healthier, more secure future where communities thrive, air is clean, and profits serve the common good, not the pockets of the few.

I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030.

This is about more than cleaner air — it’s about fairness and a secure future for everyone. Ending new petrol car sales by 2030 will cut household fuel costs, slash emissions, and speed the shift to cheaper, renewable energy. But for this to be a just transition, government must pair the ban with practical support: massive investment in affordable public transport, grants and low-interest loans for electric and shared vehicles, and a national programme to install accessible charging points — especially in social housing, rental areas and rural communities. We must protect jobs with retraining for workers in the auto and fuel industries and ensure batteries and vehicles are produced under strong environmental and labour standards. Privatised car and oil interests shouldn’t be allowed to profiteer from the switch; public ownership and strong regulation will keep prices down and benefits local. Real Hope, Real Change — a 2030 ban, backed by fair policies, gives us cleaner air, lower bills, and a secure future for our children. For the Common Good.

I strongly oppose the government’s plan to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This is another Net Zero diktat dreamed up by the Westminster bubble and forced onto ordinary, hard-working people who actually depend on their cars. For millions — rural families, farmers, tradespeople and small businesses — a petrol vehicle isn’t a luxury, it’s how they earn a living and keep their communities running. Forcing an early ban will push up costs, wreck second-hand markets, and leave people stuck with impractical, expensive alternatives that don’t work off-grid or on muddy lanes.

Worse, this is about virtue-signalling, not common sense. The “green” elites want to remake our lives while ignoring the consequences: higher bills, fewer choices, and more dependence on foreign supply chains for parts and electricity. Instead of imposed bans, we should prioritise affordable energy, expand British oil and gas production, and let people choose what’s right for their family. Scrap this ban — restore freedom, lower living costs, and put Britain’s interests first.

Ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030? I oppose it — strongly.

This isn’t about “saving the planet,” it’s about yet another Westminster diktat that punishes ordinary people. The Green Blob’s deadline would force millions to buy expensive electric cars they can’t afford, plug them into a grid taxed to death by green levies, and watch their motoring costs and household bills soar. Rural families, tradesmen and small businesses who rely on vans and longer drives will be hit hardest — electric isn’t a practical replacement for farm work or long-distance driving yet. Public transport isn’t an option for many, and charging infrastructure in the North, the Midlands and our villages is woefully inadequate.

We should be backing British energy production, cutting levies, and investing in realistic, affordable alternatives — not imposing a rushed ban that means net poverty for hardworking people. Scrap the 2030 petrol ban. Restore common sense, protect jobs and pocketbooks, and stop the war on drivers. Restore Britain’s power and prosperity.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means acting now to cut the emissions wrecking our climate and to stop sky-high petrol bills eating into family budgets. Renewable electricity and affordable electric vehicles are ready — the barrier isn’t technology, it’s a system that puts corporate profit first. A 2030 ban, paired with public investment, would scale up charging infrastructure, boost domestic green jobs, and make clean transport cheaper for everyone.

Crucially, this must be fair: invest in grants and scrappage schemes for low-income and rural households, fund community charging hubs, and expand free or low-cost public transport for young people and key workers. Public ownership of rail and local transport would lock in cheaper fares and better services. A bold deadline sends a clear signal to industry while protecting people from the transition’s costs.

For the Common Good: phase out petrol, put people first, and build Fairer, Greener Communities where every child breathes clean air and every household has a secure, affordable way to get around.
